title: Enhancing Hypnotic Medication Discontinuation in Primary Care
official: Enhancing Hypnotic Medication Discontinuation in Primary Care Through Supervised Medication Tapering and Digital Cognitive Behavioral Insomnia Therapy
summary:
Many individuals with insomnia seek treatment in primary care settings, where they often receive prescription hypnotic medications as their first and sometimes only treatment. However, extended use of these medications can lead to reliance and increased health risks, such as falls and cognitive impairments. While evidence-based approaches like physician-supervised medication tapering exist, they're not widely available in primary care or other medical clinics.

Most primary care providers are willing to explore non-drug treatments like cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBTI), but accessing such treatments can be challenging outside of specialized sleep centers. This gap between research and practice underscores the need for cost-effective interventions to manage insomnia and help patients reduce their reliance on hypnotics in primary care.

In response to this need, the project aims to conduct a large randomized trial comparing a combined digital CBT (dCBTI) and medication tapering intervention with medication tapering alone. We'll recruit 250 patients reliant on hypnotics across collaborating clinics and the general public . The main goal is to assess the effectiveness of dCBTI+SMT compared to SMT alone in reducing hypnotic use and improving insomnia symptoms.

Additionally, we'll evaluate factors affecting the adoption and implementation of these interventions at the patient, provider, and system levels. This information will inform future implementation strategies to disseminate effective treatments in primary care.

Furthermore, we'll gather data to identify which patients benefit most from dCBTI+SMT. Overall, this study will provide valuable insights into the feasibility, clinical utility, and acceptability of these interventions in managing insomnia and reducing reliance on hypnotic medications in medical settings. Ultimately, this project represents a crucial first step toward making accessible and cost-effective strategies available to improve the quality of life for millions of chronic users of sleep aids.
criteria:
Inclusion criteria will be used to enroll individuals who are: (1) 18 years of age or older; (2) able to read and effectively communicate in English (without the use of a translator), as study resources are not available in other languages; (3) able to access reliable internet and a device with web-camera and Bluetooth capabilities that can be used for virtual study visits, study survey completion, digital insomnia intervention, and app-based activity tracking; (4) an established patient with a medical provider within a healthcare practice that has been trained on structured medication taper practices by our study group or able to confirm an established relationship with a prescribing provider and is willing to involve that provider if enrolled; (5) a history of extended (≥ 3 consecutive months) and frequent (≥3 nights/week on average) use of an eligible medication (see Appendix A); (6) a desire to decrease/eliminate hypnotic use; (7) a history of insomnia that meets DSM-560 criteria for insomnia disorder (as measured by the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5, SCID98); and (8) willingness to provide written informed consent to participate.

Exclusion criteria for this study include: (1) a lifetime diagnosis of any psychotic disorder, a lifetime diagnosis of a bipolar disorder, or suicide attempts within the last 3 years; (2) presence of an unstable, untreated, or terminal medical (e.g., serious neoplastic, cardiovascular, respiratory, liver, hematological, neurodegenerative, or infectious disorders that risk the subject well-being) or psychiatric condition or symptoms that would make participation unsafe or unfeasible (as assessed by initial screening and assessment and determined by the PI and/or medical monitor when indicated), with a full list of conditions and procedures available in the manual of operations; (3) imminent risk for suicide as evidenced by endorsement of suicide item on PHQ-9 followed by a moderate to high risk determination on Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale Screen; (4) history of a seizure disorder; (5) alcohol or drug abuse within the past year;(7) use of atypically high dosages of inclusionary BZD or NBZD hypnotic medications (i.e., ≥ 10mg of diazepam equivalents/night) if, after case review and/or further clinical evaluation, is deemed by study medical staff to be at high risk for serious adverse events by participating in this study; (8) pregnancy (per self-report); (9) significant cognitive impairment as suggested by a score of \<19 on the remote adaptation of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA); (10) Current use of corticosteroids; (11) screening evidence (per Structured Clinical Interview for Sleep Disorders - Revised, SCISD-R and/or further screening by PI as needed) suggesting a current circadian rhythm disorder (e.g., delayed sleep phase type, advanced sleep phase type, shift work type, irregular-sleep wake type, non-24-hour-sleep-wake type) or other sleep disorder (i.e., narcolepsy, idiopathic hypersomnolence, REM behavior disorder, marked levels of excessive daytime sleepiness as a symptom of several potential underlying physiological sleep disorders) for which CBTI would not represent optimal therapy (12) care-taking responsibilities that cause sleep disruption;113 consuming \>2 alcoholic beverages/day ≥5 times/week. Prospective patients using alcohol specifically as a sleep aid, or alcohol after 7:00 pm more than once a week, will be required to discontinue this practice at least 1 week prior to enrollment/consent visit in order to be eligible to continue. These individuals will be asked to discontinue this practice for the remainder of the trial, although will not be removed from the study if they report use at later time points in the study.
